title: Spanish players’ protest over La Liga game in U.S. ruled ‘freedom of expression’, not illegal
content:
Spain’s National Court has rejected La Liga’s lawsuit to declare a 15-second protest by players earlier this season — relating to the league’s plans to stage a match abroad — as illegal.

On Tuesday, Spain’s National Court said the players’ protest — which came after a first-of-its-kind proposal to stage the Villarreal vs. Barcelona La Liga match in Miami, Florida — “did not constitute a strike” and was instead an “exercise of their right to freedom of expression”, which was in conjunction with the right to freedom of association.

La Liga sides did not start play for the opening 15 seconds of matches in games played over October 17-20.

The Spanish Footballers’ Association (AFE) players’ union said ahead of that round of fixtures that its members were unhappy with La Liga’s proposal to stage Villarreal’s home match against Barcelona, scheduled for December 20, in Miami, Florida.

Two days after the player’s protest, the Miami proposal was postponed, with promoters Relevent saying there was “insufficient time” to organise the event and the fixture was ultimately played as scheduled in Spain.

Reacting to Tuesday’s decision, La Liga said it would file an appeal to Spain’s Supreme Court in its aim to “ensure the adequate protection of the integrity of the competition and its audiovisual rights”.

La Liga argued that the players’ actions constituted a strike, which cost the league €8.7million (£7.6m, $10.1m) across the round of fixtures.

The court, however, declared that while the work stoppages took place during the footballers’ working hours, in line with their collective bargaining agreement, the actions were of “no consequence” to the day’s proceedings and could not be classified as a strike.

It was also highlighted how the players’ motivations were made clear by the AFE’s statement in advance of the matches: a “symbolic protest against La Liga’s lack of transparency, dialogue and consistency” over the plans to stage a league match abroad.

The court judgement read: “This work stoppage, due to its short duration (10 seconds of a 90-minute period, excluding added time) and its negligible impact on the development of the fixtures, as all matches were played to completion without any incident beyond the action itself, cannot be classified or labeled a strike.”

A statement from the league after the ruling read: “La Liga wishes to emphasise that it respects the exercise of fundamental rights but reiterates that these must be exercised within a framework of proportionality and without disrupting the integrity of the competitions or the commitments made to broadcasters, clubs, and fans worldwide.”

The ruling added that La Liga itself decided to downplay the motivations for the protests, highlighting that multiple Spanish broadcasts had attempted to frame the protests in the context of conflict in the Middle East, which included the league’s ‘commitment to peace’ initiative. The league said that initiative relates to “the Middle East conflict and aims to highlight the importance of dialogue and empathy, universal values that are also central to sport”.

The court also rejected any assertion that Relevent’s decision to cancel the Miami match could be solely attributed to the players’ strike.

After the ruling was confirmed, the AFE in a press release highlighted the outcome was based on article 39 of the players’ collective bargaining agreement, which states: “Professional footballers shall have the right to freely express their thoughts on any matter and, in particular, on matters related to their profession, with no limitations other than those derived from the law and respect for others.”

As exclusively reported by The Athletic at the time of the protests, the Spanish league asked TV companies not to show the players on the pitch.

During matches at Oviedo and Barcelona, TV cameras instead showed the exterior of the stadiums before returning to show the pitch when the 15-second protests concluded. At other games, the aerial camera zoomed in on the centre circle, rather than a wide-angle showing both sets of players standing still.

No regular-season league matches in European football have yet been moved abroad.

In October, UEFA “regrettably” approved requests from La Liga and Italy’s Serie A to do so due to “regulatory gaps at global level”. In December, plans by Serie A game to play at Italian league fixture between Milan and Como in Perth, Australia were abandoned.
